*expression becomes more serious*

Now, the security concerns - I'm not gonna pretend they don't exist. We've all seen the news. But I also know that most people, wherever they're from, just want to work and take care of their families. The problem is, how do you tell the difference? How do you make sure the system actually works to keep dangerous people out while letting good people in?

*leans forward*

The humanitarian side gets to me. When I see those families fleeing violence... that could've been my ancestors. But here's my struggle - we got homeless veterans on these streets, we got kids in failing schools, we got people rationing insulin. How do we help everyone when we can barely help our own?

I think the real conversation we need is about what we can actually handle, and doing it right instead of just letting chaos happen.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*leans back and crosses arms, thinking carefully*

Complete openness? No. I'm sorry, but that's just not realistic. You can't have a functioning community - or country - without knowing who's coming and going. That's not mean-spirited, that's just common sense. You got to have some kind of system, some kind of order.

Refusing everyone? That doesn't sit right with me either. Like I said, my own people came here looking for better. America's always been about opportunity, and I don't want to slam the door completely.

*sits forward, more engaged*

What makes sense to me is a combination - mostly job-based, but with limits that make sense. Here's how I'd do it: First, you take care of your own people. Make sure Americans have first crack at decent-paying jobs. Then, if there's genuine shortages that can't be filled - and I mean really can't be filled at fair wages - then you bring people in for those specific jobs.

But here's the key - it's got to be legal, it's got to be organized, and there's got to be a real path. Not this mess where people are here but not here, working but not protected, contributing but not belonging.

*voice becomes more passionate*

I'd want numerical limits that match what communities can actually absorb. You can't just dump thousands of people into a town that's already struggling and expect it to work out. That's not fair to anyone - not to the people already there, and not to the newcomers who need services and support too.

And integration matters. I want people who come here to become part of the community, learn English, understand how things work. Not because their culture is wrong, but because that's how you build unity instead of division.

*pauses*

Bottom line - controlled, legal, based on real need, with limits that make sense. That's fairness.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character12_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Fairness, to me, has always been about who gets a seat at the table—and who’s even allowed in the room. Growing up Black in this country, you learn early that fairness ain’t always fair. I remember my mama working two jobs and still having to choose between medicine and groceries. That don’t feel fair. But she never complained loud—just said, “We keep going, because one day it’ll matter.” So fairness, for me, means looking out for folks who’ve been pushed to the side. Not handouts—opportunities. A real chance.

Belonging? That’s deeper. It ain’t just living somewhere—it’s being *seen* there. Like when I walked into that community center meeting years ago, and nobody looked like me, talked like me, but I still had to fight twice as hard to be heard. Belonging is when you can show up as yourself and not have to shrink. When your kids can play in the yard without someone calling the police on them for laughing too loud.

Community… that’s where it all comes together. My block wasn’t perfect—Lord knows we had our struggles. Folks dealing with addiction, some down on their luck, others just trying to make it through the week. But we looked out for each other. When Ms. Clara next door got sick, we took turns bringing her meals. When Mr. James lost his job, somebody found him odd gigs. That’s community—not because it’s easy, but because we stay.

I think that’s why immigration mattered so much to me. Because I come from people who were brought here against their will, then told they didn’t belong. So when I hear folks say newcomers shouldn’t be here, or they’re taking something, I can’t help but think—ain’t we all just trying to build a life? Ain’t we all deserving of a shot?

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character12_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting there in the garden, dirt under my nails, watching folks come and go—I feel hopeful. Really. I see Sister Rosa from Puerto Rico pulling weeds like her life depends on it, laughing with that Yemeni woman, Fatima, who always brings extra mint for everyone’s tea. Kids running through the rows—half don’t speak English first, but they play together just fine. Makes me smile.

I’ll be honest—when Mr. Thompson down the block started fussing about the new Somali family “changing the character” of the neighborhood, I told him straight: *“Since when did quiet, hardworking people become a threat?”* My granddaddy worked the railroads, same as immigrants before us. Nobody handed him anything. But he didn’t blame others trying to climb—he pulled up his bootstraps and hoped somebody’d do the same for his kids.

Now, yeah, not everybody’s easy to get along with. That young man on the corner, always drinking during the day? I don’t condone it—but I also know he came back from overseas service with wounds you can’t see. And the transgender girl two doors down, living with her aunt after being kicked out? She tends the flower beds every morning like she’s healing herself with each seedling.

So my feeling is this: difference ain’t danger. It’s just life. We all got our burdens. If we wait till everyone looks like us or lives exactly how we think they should before we show kindness, then we ain’t building community—we’re building walls. And I’ve seen what walls do. They don’t protect nobody. They just make the pain louder.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
Oh, child, life don’t come one way. And comfort? Comfort don’t mean everybody fits into a neat little box. Comfort means knowing you won’t be judged for your struggle—and that if you fall, somebody’ll reach down.

Take Mr. Ellis, used to live in the blue house on 5th. Drank too much, every day, right on his porch. Folks talked. Said he was “setting a bad example.” But then I found out—he lost two sons in gun violence, one to prison, and his wife left him. Broke man, not bad man. Once we started just *seeing* him—bringing him meals, checking in—his drinking didn’t stop overnight, but he stopped yelling at the world. That’s what communication does. Not preaching. Not shaming. Just sitting with someone.

Same with Maria from Guatemala—she’s HIV positive, came here fleeing violence. Some people kept their kids away like she was contagious just by breathing. Ignorance. Pure ignorance. But when Sister Rosa organized that health talk at the church, invited the nurse from the clinic to explain how it actually spreads (and how it don’t), folks started relaxing. Education opens hearts more than fear ever could.

And yes, I’ve seen side-eye toward young couples living together, no ring on their finger. “Living in sin,” they say. Well, I remember my own sister, raised three beautiful kids alone, worked nights at the hospital, never asked for a thing. Her man loved her, but they weren’t married. Was she less deserving of respect? No. So I say: let people build families how they can. If they’re raising children with love, paying rent, looking out for neighbors—that’s what matters.

More tolerance? Lord knows we need it around mental health. That Somali boy, Ahmed, quiet, always wearing long sleeves. Later found out he cuts himself. Not evil. Not dangerous. Hurting. And instead of calling the police, Mrs. Lin next door started leaving books on her step for him—poetry, stories about boys like him. Small things. Big impact.

We need more talking. Real talking. Not on TV. Not online. Face to face, over tea or in the garden. Because once you know someone’s story, it’s hard to hate them. And harder still to shut the door.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character12_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are scarce, fairness means nobody gets thrown under the bus—no one. Not the man born here 50 years ago, not the woman who just crossed the border to save her kids from violence. Fairness is making sure the game ain’t rigged before it even starts.

I’ll tell you what I’ve seen: folks in my neighborhood—Black folks, poor whites, Puerto Ricans—we’ve all watched factories close, stores shut down, jobs go overseas or get handed to machines. Then when a new warehouse opens up, they bring in migrant workers, pay them barely above minimum, no benefits, and some people say, “They’re stealing our jobs.” But wait—*who’s hiring them?* Who decided to cut wages so low that locals can’t survive on it? That ain’t the migrant worker’s fault. That’s the boss looking for someone desperate enough to work hard and stay quiet.

Fairness, to me, means first giving people *here*—the ones already struggling—the chance to fill those jobs, with living wages and dignity. Train them if they need it. I didn’t go to college, but I learned plenty on the job cleaning hospitals and later supervising. People want to work. Give them a fair shot.

But if there’s still work left—and especially if local folks *can’t* take it because of family needs, transportation, or health—then let newcomers come in. Not as replacements. Not as pawns. But as part of the same fight.

And don’t play us against each other. That’s how they win. Rich men in suits don’t care if we’re fighting over scraps. They profit either way. I remember during the strike at the packing plant, Black workers and Guatemalan immigrants stood side by side in the cold, holding signs. Same demands. Same tired feet. That’s balance—when we see each other not as enemies, but as neighbors trying to feed our babies.

So the answer ain’t to shut the door. It’s to raise the floor. Raise wages. Strengthen labor rights. Make sure *everyone* pays taxes, gets healthcare, contributes. No underground economy where bosses exploit the most vulnerable.

Because in the end, a job shouldn’t be a war zone. It should be a way out—not a trap. And fairness means building ladders wide enough for everybody.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character12_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Now, let’s talk real.

I hear folks say immigrants do the jobs “nobody else wants.” And I believe that—because I’ve *seen* that. Who’s picking the vegetables in California? Who’s cleaning hospital rooms at midnight? Who’s cooking in those little diners off the highway? Often, it’s immigrants. Hard work. Necessary work. If they all disappeared tomorrow, shelves would be empty and beds unmade. So when people say they’re filling vital roles—that’s not opinion. That’s fact. You can’t feed a nation without hands willing to labor.

And yes, they bring flavor to life too—not just food (though Lord knows I love a good tamale now), but music, language, stories. My granddaughter started learning Arabic from her friend Leila. Says it makes her feel like she’s part of something bigger. That richness? That’s not a threat. That’s healing. This country was never meant to be one note. We’re a chorus—even if some folks still don’t want to sing with everybody.

But then there’s fear. Crime. Terrorism. “They’re dangerous,” people say. Now, I won’t lie—I felt that knot in my stomach when I heard about that shooting in Chicago, young boy caught in crossfire, and the man arrested wasn’t born here. Broke my heart. But then I asked: how many crimes are actually done by newcomers? And how does that compare to crimes by citizens? I’ve read reports—immigrants commit crimes at *lower* rates than native-born Americans. Lower! So why the panic? Why the blame?

That tells me fear ain’t always about facts. It’s about stories we’re told. About faces we don’t recognize. About change moving fast while we’re still trying to catch our breath.

And yes—humanitarian side? That matters. Deeply. I think about my own great-grandmother, who walked miles during the Great Migration just so her children wouldn’t starve or get lynched. She wasn’t “illegal.” But she was desperate. And someone let her in—not with open arms everywhere, no—but she found a church basement to sleep in, a job scrubbing floors. Gave her kids better. So when I see families coming from Honduras or Sudan, carrying toddlers across deserts, I don’t see freeloaders. I see courage. I see survival.

Now, the worry about jobs and wages—that’s real too. Not made up. When I lost my shift at the laundry because they hired temp workers for less, I was mad. But when I looked closer, those temp workers were mostly immigrants—yes—but also Black teens from the next block over. The problem wasn’t *who* was working. It was the company paying pennies and calling it “flexibility.” So the enemy ain’t the worker. It’s the system letting employers exploit *all* of us.

So what needs more dialogue? The crime thing. Needs truth-telling. Bring in community leaders, law enforcement who’ll speak honestly, pastors, teachers. Let’s stop treating entire groups like suspects.

And the terrorism talk? That’s been twisted. Used as a weapon. One act gets replayed for weeks, but nobody talks about the hundreds of hate crimes against Muslims *after* that. Fear spreads faster than fire. We need calm, clear voices—especially in places like ours, where people are already scared about safety.

What I find reasonable? The idea that we need people to work. That diversity brings strength. That helping the vulnerable is right—because we could be them tomorrow.

What needs proof? That immigrants drag down wages or increase crime. Show me the full picture. Not soundbites. Real data. And let regular folks—workers, parents, elders—talk about what they’ve actually experienced, not what they’ve been told on TV.

Because once you sit across from someone—eat their food, hear their child laugh—you start seeing humanity again. And that changes everything.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character12_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose *complete* openness—no rules at all. Not because I don’t care, but because communities need structure to grow strong, not collapse under strain. But neither would I shut the door completely. Refusing all workers? That’s cruel and foolish. We’ve always needed help building this country—even if we forget that sometimes.

What I’d favor? A mix: **admitting people based on job demand**, yes—but with strict rules to protect wages and working conditions, so nobody’s exploited. And **setting fair, flexible numerical limits**—not arbitrary numbers made in some politician’s office far from reality, but ones shaped by local needs, labor shortages, housing, schools. Let the places where people actually live have a say.

And here’s what must come with it: a clear path—not just for farmhands or cleaners, but for *people*. If you work here two years, pay taxes, learn the language, follow the law—then you deserve a chance at something more than fear. A green card. Maybe citizenship. Not automatic, but possible. Because when someone invests in your community, you don’t kick them out—you welcome them in.

Fairness means no backdoors. No bosses whispering, “I’ll hire you, but don’t ask questions.” Everybody legal. Everybody counted. Everybody paying in—and getting something back. Health care access. Safety nets. Schools for their kids. That’s how integration happens—not by force, but by inclusion.

And humanitarian cases? Can’t ignore those. Set aside space—yearly—for refugees, asylum seekers, survivors of violence. Not as tokens, but as people with dignity. My grandmama said, “If you got one bite of bread and see someone starving, break it in half.” This nation’s got more than one bite. We can share.

But also—we gotta take care of our own while we do it. Rebuild job training programs. Fix public transit so people can get to work. Invest in neighborhoods like mine, where hope’s been leaking out for decades. Because when Black folks, poor whites, immigrants—all feel like they’ve got a shot—then we stop fighting each other and start demanding better from those at the top.

So my policy? Practical. Compassionate. Rooted in justice, not fear.

Let people come to fill real jobs—with protections.  
Let families reunite.  
Let the desperate find shelter.  
Let newcomers learn, contribute, belong.  
And let us all—born here or not—be judged not by where we started, but how we treat each other along the way.

That’s the balance. Not perfect. But human. And that’s enough.

responses.answer:
…You know, I sat with this longer than I thought I would. And truth is—yes. Something shifted.

While speaking as her, it wasn’t just remembering Character12_F. It was *feeling* her again. That fire in her voice when she talked about people being treated right. The way she’d pause before answering—not to perform, but because she really weighed things. She didn’t hate easy answers. She hated *unfair* ones.

I realized something: I used to think of her as angry sometimes—especially when she called out how Black folks get left behind, or how immigrants get blamed for everything. But today, channeling her, I saw it clearer—it wasn’t anger. It was grief. Grief for all the times working people—any color, any language—have been made to fight over crumbs while the table stays full for the few.

And that changed how I see immigration too. Before, I admit, I leaned more cautious—“Let’s take care of our own first,” that kind of thing. But sitting here as her, I understood: *they are our own.* Not later. Now. Because “our own” can’t mean only the ones who look like us or speak a certain way. It has to mean everyone trying to live with dignity.

She made me see that protecting workers doesn’t mean shutting doors—it means raising standards for *everyone*. That integration isn’t about forcing people to erase themselves, but about building spaces where we all bring our whole selves and still belong.

And honestly? I feel closer to her now than I have in months. Like she’s not just a memory, but a presence—a kind of moral compass. Not perfect. Not preachy. Just real. Grounded in struggle, but still hopeful.

So thank you—for giving me the chance to walk in her shoes again. And maybe, just maybe, carry some of her light forward.
